Named in honour of its inventor Waloddi Weibull who introduced it for the first time in 1939 in connection with
his studies on the strength of materials (see Weibull (1939)), this distribution is widely used as a model in reliability
and lifetime studies (see Lawless (1982); Murthy et al. (2004); Nelson (1982)). There are many applications of the
Weibull distribution in medicine, biology, agriculture, forestry and engineering sciences. In addition, the Weibull
distribution has found applications as a trend curve in much applied research (see Banks (1994); Ross (1990); Seber

Unfortunately, none of these methods (excluding the Bayesian one) is appropriate for small data sets (see Lawless
A very popular method for parameter estimation is the least squares (LS) method. Numerical methods for solving
the nonlinear LS problem are described in Dennis and Schnabel (1996); Gill et al. (1981). Before the iterative
minimization of the sum of squares it is still necessary to ask whether the least squares estimate (LSE) exists. In
the case of nonlinear LS problems it is still extremely difficult to answer this question (see Bates and Watts (1988);
Bjorck¨ (1996); Demidenko (2006, 2000); Hadeler et al. (2007); Jukic´ et al. (2004, 1999)).
Surprisingly, in spite of the many papers on Weibull models, we have not managed to find any paper dealing with
the existence problem for a solution to a nonlinear LS problem for the three-parametric Weibull distribution.
The structure of the paper is as follows. In Section 2 we present our main result (Theorem 1) which guarantees
the existence of the LSE for the three-parametric Weibull distribution. An illustrative numerical example is given in
Section 3. To avoid nonnecessary technicalities at an early stage, all proofs are given in Section 4.
